Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Review the epidemiology, etiology, and risk factors associated with claw toe deformity and
hammer toe deformity.
Perform an appropriate workup for patients with claw toe deformity and patients with
hammer toe deformity.
Explain the surgical and nonsurgical management of claw toe deformity and hammer toe
deformity.
Claw Toe Deformity
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy

The primary deficiency at the metatarsophalangeal (MTP) joint level is dysfunction or tearing of
the plantar plate, which usually holds the base of the phalanx in alignment with the metatarsal
head.1
Claw toe is an extension deformity at the MTP joint combined with hyperflexion at the
proximal interphalangeal (PIP) and distal interphalangeal (DIP) joints. The deformity may be
flexible or fixed (Table 1).
The difference between a hammer toe and a claw toe is the positioning of the DIP joint1.
The DIP joint is flexed in a patient with a claw toe deformity.
The DIP joint is extended in a patient with hammer toe deformity.
Lesser toe deformity has a wide spectrum of underlying pathology and includes static and
dynamic deformity. In addition, severity can vary substantially, from synovitis to MTP joint
dislocation. Understanding the anatomy and biomechanics underlying the deformity allows for
targeted management and more predictable outcomes (Figure 1 ; Resource 1).

Anatomy and Biomechanics
Osteology
Lesser metatarsals articulate with the base of the lesser proximal phalanges.
Vascular Structures
The plantar arch is the circular anastomosis formed by the deep plantar branch of the dorsalis
pedis artery and the lateral plantar artery.
Supplies the plantar aspect of the distal foot and the lesser toes
Arcuate artery (branch of the dorsalis pedis artery)
Supplies the dorsal aspect of the distal foot, lesser toes, and web spaces
Microvascular network extends from the surrounding soft tissues at the attachments of the
plantar plate on the metatarsal and the proximal phalanx.2
The midsubstance of the plantar plate is hypovascular.2
Vascular density is increased at the proximal and distal aspects of the plantar plate.2

Nerves
The dorsal sensory and plantar digital nerves supply the lesser digits and the MTP joint
articulation.
Tendons
The central dorsal structure of the toe is formed by the extensor digitorum longus (EDL), which
divides into three slips over the proximal phalanx.
The middle slip inserts into the base of the middle phalanx.
Two lateral slips extend over the dorsolateral aspect of the middle phalanx and converge to
form the terminal tendon, which inserts into the base of the distal phalanx.
The EDL is held in a central position dorsally by a fibroaponeurotic sling that anchors to the
plantar aspect of the MTP joint and the base of the proximal phalanx.

MTP

Connects the head of the metatarsals
Attaches to the plantar plate
Flexor tendons cross the TML plantarly.
Interossei cross the TML dorsally.

Etiology
Synovitis is the most common cause.
Because of overuse, shoe wear, inflammatory disease, hallux valgus, and other factors
Trauma

Natural History
Typically involves multiple and bilateral lesser toe joints.
May involve a single toe
Deformity often is progressive.
As the claw toe develops, the flexor tendons pull the interphalangeal joints into flexion and the
MTP joint into extension.
This results in depression of the metatarsal head and pulling of the plantar fat pad distally.
May result in metatarsalgia, callus, or ulcer formation

Cavus deformity
Classification
Static (fixed, irreducible) versus dynamic (flexible, reducible) deformity
Staging of MTP joint instability4 (Resource 2)
Stage 0: no malalignment; presence of prodromal pain.
Stage 1: mild malalignment; widening of web space.
Stage 2: moderate malalignment; more than 50% subluxation with the drawer test.
Stage 3: severe malalignment; dorsal deformity; dislocation with the drawer test.
Stage 4: severe malalignment; dislocation; fixed hammer toe.

Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Claw toe deformity involves an imbalance of intrinsic and extrinsic muscles. The EDL is
substantially more powerful than the antagonistic intrinsic muscles crossing the MTP
joint, and these structures, along with the collateral ligaments and the plantar plate
complex, affect the position of this joint. The EDL extends the MTP joint through a
fibroaponeurotic sling attached to the plantar plate and capsule. The EDL can assist with
extension of the interphalangeal joints of the lesser toes only if the MTP joint is in a
neutral or flexed position. Hyperextension of the MTP joint and subsequent dorsal
translation of the proximal phalangeal base shifts the flexion moment arm dorsally,
which decreases the strength of the extrinsic muscles and allows for the relative overpull
of the intrinsic muscles. The EDL then becomes a deforming force on the MTP joint.
Flexion of the MTP joint primarily is a function of the intrinsic muscles. The plantar and
dorsal interossei aid in flexion of the MTP joint because the axis of pull is plantar to the
center of rotation if the joint is in a neutral position. As the MTP joint becomes
chronically extended, the stabilizing structures (collateral ligaments and plantar plate)
attenuate, and these tendons become a force of dorsal subluxation5 (Resource 3).
Evaluation/Diagnosis

Pathology
Deformities of the lesser toes result from an imbalance between the intrinsic and extrinsic
musculotendinous units of the toes.
With hyperextension at the MTP joint, the strong flexors overpower the intrinsic extensors of
the interphalangeal joints.
This results in flexion deformities at the interphalangeal joints and extension deformities at
the MTP joints.
The primary deficiency at the MTP joint level is dysfunction or rupture of the plantar plate.9

A single injection followed by protected ambulation may be beneficial.

Indications
Nonsurgical treatment should be attempted in almost all symptomatic patients.
Exception
Acute injury resulting in deformity may require surgical management.

Techniques/Procedures
The MTP joint imbalance may be addressed via extensor tendon Z-plasty lengthening
and MTP joint capsular release; however, the surgeon should take care to not create an
extensor lag. A distal oblique metatarsal shortening osteotomy often is performed to
access the plantar plate or to improve stability of reduction and can be translated in the
axial plane to aid in deformity correction (ie, medializing Weil osteotomy).12 This also can
be accomplished with a slightly more proximal distal metaphyseal metatarsal osteotomy.
In patients with an increased risk for wound problems, this may be performed
percutaneously.
FDL to EDL (Girdlestone-Taylor) tendon transfer or extensor digitorum brevis tendon
transfer under the TML may be performed to achieve balance in the flexible claw toe.14
If the deformity has a crossover component, the damaged collateral ligament is repaired
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:33 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003002

with the use of nonabsorbable suture, and the contracted (opposite) collateral ligament
is released. A Kirschner wire (K-wire) often is used to maintain correction.
The plantar plate may be repaired directly via a dorsal approach (often requiring a
metatarsal shortening osteotomy) or a plantar approach. Newer procedures include
repair of the plantar plate at the proximal phalanx plantar insertion.11 The plantar plate
is captured with the use of a nonabsorbable suture via a suture passer system. The
suture is then passed through drill holes in the base of the proximal phalanx and tied
dorsally with the toe positioned in slight plantar flexion.
Preoperative Planning
Note the metatarsal head cascade.
Do not over-shorten the metatarsal via osteotomy.
The position of the hallux may impair correction of the lesser MTP deformity. The hallux may
need to be aligned to allow for lesser toe correction.(Figure 10)

Dorsal
Straight or lazy-S incision
Centered over the affected MTP joint for a single toe
Centered in the web space for two toes
Tenotomy of the extensor brevis and Z-lengthening of the extensor longus aid in reduction

Plantar
Straight longitudinal
Centered over the affected metatarsal head for a single toe
Centered in the web space for two toes

Attain hemostasis before closure because hematoma formation in this area may lead to
wound complications.
Postoperative Management
A well-padded forefoot dressing is applied.
This dressing may be used to maintain correction but should not be used to gain correction.
Most patients are allowed to bear weight on the heel in an open-toed, hard-soled shoe after 72
hours of elevation.
Sutures are removed and a new forefoot dressing is applied 10 to 14 days postoperatively.
Patients may then bear weight as tolerated in an open-toed, hard-soled shoe.
The dressing and pin (if used) are removed at 5 to 6 weeks postoperatively, and the patient is
transitioned to a wide, stiff-soled shoe.

Outcomes

Outcomes
Although often unsuccessful in correcting deformity, nonsurgical management usually
allows for adequate symptom relief to avoid surgical managment.22 Surgical
management may be considered if nonsurgical management is unsuccessful. Most
common surgical treatment options are associated with good results and high patient
satisfaction. Flint et al10 reported 80% good to excellent results with primary plantar
plate repair via a dorsal approach with a Weil osteotomy. Independently, excellent
results have been reported with a Weil metatarsal osteotomy23 and a slightly more
proximal distal metatarsal metaphyseal osteotomy. In patients with an increased risk of
wound issues, a percutaneous technique has been described with satisfactory results.13
Although flexor-to-extensor transfer often results in satisfactory outcomes, Myerson and
Jung24 reported a fairly high rate of complications and patient dissatisfaction.
Hammer Toe Deformity
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
Hammer toe is a flexion deformity at the PIP joint and an extension deformity at the MTP and
DIP joints (Figure 11).

Hammer toe is the most common deformity observed in the lesser toes.
The difference between a hammer toe and a claw toe is the positioning of the DIP joint.25
The DIP joint is flexed with a claw toe deformity.
The DIP joint is extended with a hammer toe deformity.
Figure 11 Clinical photograph of a foot shows a hammer toe deformity. (Courtesy of David R.
Richardson, MD, Southaven, MS.)

Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Hammer toe is used to describe the abnormal flexion posture of the lesser toes. This
deformity may be fixed or flexible and may be associated with a rotational component
(most often occurring in the fifth digit). Lesser toe deformity is associated with a wide
spectrum of underlying pathology. In addition, severity may vary substantially from
synovitis to joint dislocation,. Understanding the anatomy and biomechanics underlying
the deformity allows for targeted management and more predictable outcomes.

Increased incidence with advancing age
Peaking in individuals in their fifties and sixties
More common in women than men

Classification
Flexible or rigid
Most hammer toe deformities are not associated with underlying intrinsic imbalance or
neuromuscular disease. The intrinsic musculature of the foot essentially has no activity
during the first 35% of the gait cycle.4 Hammer toe deformity usually worsens with
standing and, therefore, is not a function of intrinsic muscle balance.
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
Clinical presentation includes pain and callus formation over the dorsum of the PIP joint along
with difficulty with shoe wear.
Physical Examination

Plantar flexion of the ankle corrects flexible deformity but does not alter fixed deformity.
The flexed interphalangeal joints tend to rub against the toe box of the shoe, resulting in callus
formation and pain.

Distal oblique metatarsal shortening osteotomy (Weil osteotomy)
May be modified by translating the metatarsal head medially or laterally to assist with axial
plane deformity (Figure 8)

Techniques/Procedures
In the absence of MTP joint pathology, surgical correction of hammer toes involves
resection of the distal condyles of the proximal phalanx of the toe. Resection may be
combined with FDL tenotomy, performed via the dorsal incision used for condylar
resection or via plantar percutaneous release. The toe may be pinned via temporary wire
fixation.32 PIP joint arthroplasty and fusion are associated with similar satisfaction
rates.33 Newer permanent implants are available to eliminate the need for K-wire
fixation. Numerous studies have shown only minimal improvement in patient
satisfaction without improvement in clinical outcomes but at a substantially higher cost
for the implants.34,35 If the MTP joint is involved, correction is the same as that
described for claw toe deformity.
If MTP joint deformity is present, it must be addressed. This deformity often is addressed
via a distal metatarsal osteotomy and/or plantar plate repair to improve stability of the
reduction. The Weil osteotomy is a short oblique osteotomy that, in addition to
shortening, allows for the capital fragment (metatarsal head) to be translated in the axial
plane to aid in deformity correction. The plantar plate may be repaired directly via a
dorsal approach (often requiring a metatarsal shortening osteotomy) or a plantar
approach. Newer techniques include repairing the plantar plate at the proximal phalanx
plantar insertion. The plantar plate is captured with the use of a nonabsorbable suture
via a suture passer system. The suture is then passed through drill holes in the base of
the proximal phalanx and tied dorsally with the toe positioned in slight plantar flexion.
Preoperative Planning
Note the metatarsal head cascade.
The hallux may need to be aligned to allow for lesser toe correction.
The surgical plan is based on deformity and rigidity.

Outcomes of nonsurgical management depend on several factors, including severity of
deformity, comorbidities, and compliance with the use of pads and shoe-wear
modifications. Surgical management via PIP joint arthroplasty (or fusion) is associated
with good results.32 Age does not appear to substantially diminish patient satisfaction
with surgical treatment.29 Management with the use of an exposed K-wire is associated
with low complication rates and high patient satisfaction.30 Whether the PIP joint fuses
or a stable arthroplasty forms does not appear to affect outcomes.33
